name: Kakabe
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Kakabe (kaka1265, Mande) is not in the catalog. The sweep list holds one item, Vydrina's 2017 INALCO thesis (HAL tel-03203594, open access), already on file from an earlier pass at together with four of her Mandenkan articles (2008, 2013, 2015, 2023); I re-read the thesis text layer and appended a dated sweep note to there. The thesis describes a terraced H/L tone language with the mora as TBU and states explicitly (p. 187) that Kakabe has moraic-trochee foot structure of the kind found 'in languages without phonetic stress'; tonal oppositions are 'not restricted to one culminative syllable within a prosodic word' (p. 23); the trochaic foot plays no role in vowel omission (p. 189). All other 'stress' tokens concern French, Pular, Pirahã, Russian or English. No first-hand word-stress rule exists for Kakabe in any opened source; the language belongs in the tone/no-word-stress class, so nothing needs acquiring (priority none). The earlier pass's unread wishlist (Vydrina 2017 Russian sketch in Jazyki mande; Vydrin & Vydrina 2010 JLC, DOI 10.1163/19552629-90000006, paywalled; Keita 1977, print only) is not a stress-title hit and is unlikely to change this. the HAL PDF URL was verified live (HTTP 200).

new_statements.quote: [p. 187] It has been shown that foot structure can be present in languages without phonetic stress. Kakabe is a language with moraic trochees, so that in a binary moraic foot, first mora is stronger. [p. 23] […] its tonology is different from the cases like Swedish and Japanese since the tonal oppositions are not restricted to one culminative syllable within a prosodic word. [p. 667] Kakabe is a terraced‐level tone language (H vs. L), featuring downdrift, downstep, H raising, floating L, and a number of tonal processes

new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kakabe is a two-tone (H/L) terraced-level tone language whose tone-bearing unit is the mora. Vydrina claims no phonetic word stress: metrical structure exists only as abstract moraic trochees (binary moraic feet parsed from the left edge of the prosodic word, first mora strong), which condition segmental allomorphy (diminutive -nden, vowel lengthening) and the alignment of the OCP-inserted H tone (§5.5.6: foot boundary after a heavy CVV/CVN syllable, or before the syllable with the stronger onset), not an audible accent. No culminative prominence per word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; no stress at all is described.
new_statements.exceptions: Bimoraic minimal-word requirement for prosodically independent words, with monosyllabic verbs alternating long/short vowel as the exception (p. 187); foot parsing of trisyllabic L-toned nouns varies with syllable weight and onset strength, e.g. jàmana 'land' realized with H on 2nd or 3rd syllable (§5.5.6, pp. 407-410).
new_statements.domain_note: Prosodic word is the parsing domain for feet and the domain of tonal compounding; tonal processes are phrasal (PhP/IP). Statement is about the language in general (Nuclear Kakabe, corpus mainly Central Kakabe); the stress claim is made in passing, not as a dedicated section.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes Nuclear Kakabe as a three-dialect continuum (Central, Northern, Western; §1.3.7, p. 43); the corpus and the prosodic description rest mainly on Central Kakabe (Sokotoro, Mansaya villages) with Northern/Western variation noted. All maps to language-level kaka1265; no dialect glottocodes assigned here.

new_statements.quote: Kakabe is a weight-measuring language [...] Mora functions as a tone-bearing unit. [...] It has been shown that foot structure can be present in languages without phonetic stress. Kakabe is a language with moraic trochees, so that in a binary moraic foot, first mora is stronger. Another foot-based phenomenon is the allomorphy pattern of the diminutive suffix -nden, described in Section 4.3.4. Apart from that, the alignment of separating H tone can also be foot-sensitive, see Section 5.5.6. (p. 187) [...] its tonology is different from the cases like Swedish and Japanese since the tonal oppositions are not restricted to one culminative syllable within a prosodic word. (p. 23)
new_statements.citation: Vydrina, Alexandra (2017). A corpus-based description of Kakabe, a Western Mande language: prosody in grammar. PhD thesis, INALCO (LLACAN), Paris. HAL tel-03203594.
new_statements.locator: Ch. 3 §3.3 'Phonotactic patterns', p. 187 (pdf p. 190); supporting: §1.1.3 p. 23 (pdf p. 26), §3.3.1.1 p. 189 (pdf p. 191)
new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by the language's only modern describer: Kakabe is a lexical/grammatical tone language (H/L, mora-timed) with abstract left-aligned moraic-trochee foot structure but no phonetic word stress; the feet surface only in minimal-word size, diminutive allomorphy and H-tone alignment, not in vowel reduction (p. 189). No syllable is singled out as culminative. For the stress catalog this is a 'no word stress / tone language' record, not a stress-placement coding.

sources.note: Introduction §2.3 'Le système tonal' (pp. 10-11): L and H tones plus a super-high tone on intensifiers/ideophones/quantifiers; L-toned words get LH variant before another L; downdrift; boundary tones. Stress/accent not mentioned.

sources.note: 'Comme pratiquement toutes les langues mandé, le kakabé est une langue tonale. Est attestée une opposition de deux tons, haut et bas' (p. 147). Compares loss of lexical tone under grammaticalization to loss of accent in accent languages (p. 169); no Kakabe stress statement.
